hints: Focus on what the letters in $S_N1$ really tell you about how the halogenoalkane breaks apart first.
Remember the slow step forms a carbocation, $\text{R}_3\text{C}^+$, from just the halogenoalkane alone.
Think about how alkyl groups push electrons toward a positive carbon and why that makes tertiary halogenoalkanes react fastest.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two steps of $S_N1$**

Think of $S_N1$ as substitution, nucleophilic, unimolecular. Step 1 is slow heterolysis of the $\text{C-X}$ bond to give a carbocation and $\text{X}^-$. Step 2 is fast attack by the nucleophile.

$$\text{R}_3\text{C-X} \rightarrow \text{R}_3\text{C}^+ + \text{X}^-$$

**Identify the key intermediate**

The intermediate is the carbocation, $\text{R}_3\text{C}^+$. It is formed from one molecule only, the halogenoalkane, so the slow step is unimolecular. It clearly carries a positive charge.

**Explain the stability trend**

A positive carbon is electron deficient and is stabilised by electron donation from adjacent alkyl groups. This is the positive inductive effect, so tertiary carbocations are most stable and tertiary halogenoalkanes favour $S_N1$.

options.A: Incorrect. In nucleophilic substitution, it is the leaving group (the halide, an electrophile leaving as $\text{X}^-$) that is substituted by the nucleophile, not the other way round. This option reverses the roles.
options.B: Incorrect. The rate-determining step and the intermediate formation involve only one molecule, the halogenoalkane. That is why it is called unimolecular (1 in $S_N1$). Two molecules meet only in the fast second step.
options.C: Correct. The intermediate is a carbocation which is stabilised by electron-donating adjacent alkyl groups through the positive inductive effect. More alkyl groups means a more stable intermediate and a faster $S_N1$ reaction.
options.D: Incorrect. The carbocation intermediate, $\text{R}_3\text{C}^+$, is positively charged. Heterolysis of $\text{C-X}$ gives $\text{R}^+$ and $\text{X}^-$, so charge is created in step 1.
